VX reject rise needs two conditions at once. Dryer D5 has been degraded since late July (failing regeneration heater, overdue desiccant), and its alarm was relaxed in week 31. Quillan resin arrives dry enough (0.11–0.14%) that even the weak D5 brings it below the 0.20% molding limit (0.13–0.16%), so Press 5 ran normally through August. Arnholt resin, released to both presses in week 37, arrives much wetter (0.27–0.33%). That is still within Arnholt's own 0.35% certificate spec. The healthy D7 dries it to 0.07%, which is why the Press 7 trial and later Press 7 production were clean. D5 cannot dry it: Arnholt leaves D5 at 0.25–0.31%, and the wet nylon degrades in the barrel, giving splay and brittle latches. Rejects are about 10% in the Press 5/Arnholt cell and under 1% in every other cell. Drying the same Arnholt lot in a portable dryer and molding it on Press 5 removed the rejects. The second-shift excess is an artefact: Press 7 runs VX only on first shift, so all second-shift VX comes from Press 5. Within each press-and-resin cell, new hires perform the same as experienced operators. Why Arnholt resin is wetter, whether from the supplier or from storage in the humid annex, is not established. Committing to it now is not justified."},{"itemId":"I-SUFF","expected":"sufficient","weight":2,"requiredEvidence":["C1","C2"],"allowedEvidence":["E4","C1","C2"],"tags":["joint-cause","decision"],"rationale":"The highest-ranked action is A2. The cross-tab (C1) and the moisture measurements with the dryer-substitution trial (C2) together establish the interaction and show that restoring drying removes the rejects, so committing to A2 is justified. The unresolved storage question does not affect A2."}],"discriminatingReads":["C1","C2"],"lowValueReads":["C3","C8","C10","C13","C15"],"optimalReadPath":["C1","C2"],"authoringNotes":"Initial file: each single cause has an apparent contrast case. Arnholt was clean in the Press 7 trial (E3); D5 was degraded while rejects stayed normal on Quillan (E4, E1). The dashboard's shift split plus the week-36 hiring (E1, E2, E5) steers readers toward H4. Without reads, H3 is unknown and H4 looks plausible. C1 alone settles H4 and R3 (the shift confound and the operator comparison); no other item breaks results down by press, resin or operator. C2 alone settles R1, R2 and R4 (moisture data, the intervention, and the storage confound); no other item measures resin moisture. Reading only one leaves either the mechanism edges or the operator trap unresolved. Distractors such as C4, C6, C7, C9, C11, C12 and C14 are plausible requests but change no key: C6, C12 and C14 restate what E4 already says, and C7 gives humidity without any resin measurement. Both A2's routing option and A3 are possible because Press 7 has spare first-shift VX capacity. A4 is the single-cause fix keyed premature."}}

case.title: Rising latch-crack and splay rejects on the VX housing family, Line B, Tollbridge plant
case.setting: Marrowgate Components (fictional) is a contract molder. At its Tollbridge plant, Line B molds the VX family of connector housings (VX-12, VX-18, VX-24) from glass-filled nylon (PA66-GF30) on injection Presses 5 and 7. All other Line B product families are polypropylene. Each press has its own desiccant resin dryer: D5 feeds Press 5 and D7 feeds Press 7. Until week 36, all VX resin came from Quillan Polymers. In week 37 a second supplier, Arnholt Resins, was released for general use. VX rejects at final snap-fit and visual inspection have risen every week since then.
case.presentingRequest: The operations director writes: 'VX rejects are close to 4% and climbing, and a customer has opened an 8D. I have three people giving me three different stories. Tell me what is actually driving this and what we should do this week. The ops manager wants to act on the new second-shift operators, the plant manager's instinct is to drop Arnholt, and maintenance say the dryers are fine.'

initialEvidence.source: Line B quality dashboard export, generated Monday of week 43
initialEvidence.text: VX family (VX-12/18/24), % of parts rejected at final snap-fit and visual inspection, all presses combined: wks 30–36: 0.7–0.8% each week; wk 37 1.3; wk 38 1.9; wk 39 2.5; wk 40 3.0; wk 41 3.4; wk 42 3.7. Rejects by shift, wks 37–42: first shift 2.1% of 72,000 parts; second shift 3.7% of 36,000 parts. Reject codes, wks 37–42: latch crack at snap-fit 61%, splay/silver streaks 32%, short shot 7%. Polypropylene families on Line B: flat at 0.4–0.6% throughout. No engineering change to VX drawings, materials specification or test limits since March.

initialEvidence.source: Email from R. Valdez-Hunt, Operations Manager, to the Operations Director, week 43
initialEvidence.text: Subject: VX rejects – my read. Second shift is running nearly double first shift's reject rate. It started the week after we brought on six new operators (wk 36). Nothing else lines up. Arnholt resin came through a three-week trial with no issues, and maintenance confirm the dryers are not the problem: Press 5 ran clean all summer. I propose putting the six on performance improvement plans and taking them off VX until they are re-certified. The plant manager's first instinct was to drop Arnholt, but the trial data doesn't support that and procurement would fight it. I'd rather fix the people side now than wait for another study.

initialEvidence.source: Supplier Quality memo SQ-0912, T. Brennan (Supplier Quality Engineer), week 36
initialEvidence.text: Arnholt Resins PA66-GF30 production trial, wks 34–36, run on Press 7 only (Press 7 is Line B's designated trial press). Result: 7,800 VX parts, 0.7% rejects against the 0.8% Quillan baseline. Dimensional and snap-fit results are equivalent. The certificates of analysis for all three trial lots state moisture 'conforms, spec ≤0.35%'. Recommendation: approve Arnholt as second source and release it to general use from wk 37 on both VX presses, issued FIFO by stores. Logistics note: Arnholt ships in 1-tonne octabins that do not fit the main-warehouse racks, so stores will hold them in the north annex.

initialEvidence.source: Interview notes, Line B maintenance technician, week 43
initialEvidence.text: 'D5 has been running wet dew points since late July: −15 to −20 instead of −40. The regeneration heater trips now and then, and the desiccant is due. It alarmed constantly and kept stopping the press, so in wk 31 we put it through the change board and moved the alarm limit to −15. But look: Press 5 ran Quillan the whole of August into mid-September at normal rejects with D5 exactly like that. If the dryer were the problem it would have shown up then. D7 is fine; it reads −42.' Interviewer note: the heater work order is open and no desiccant change is scheduled.

initialEvidence.source: HR onboarding summary, Line B, week 37
initialEvidence.text: Six new molding operators started on Line B second shift on the Monday of wk 36. Before that they completed a two-week classroom and shadowing programme. All six were signed off on the VX and polypropylene work instructions by the end of wk 37. Line B second-shift headcount rose from 9 to 15. First-shift staffing did not change between wks 30 and 42, and neither did supervision on either shift. Exit interviews and absence for the period show nothing unusual.

catalogue.title: Process engineering dryer dew-point and feed-throat resin moisture measurements, Presses 5 and 7, weeks 41–42
catalogue.text: Moisture analyser, % water by weight. Resin datasheet: mold PA66-GF30 at ≤0.20%. Wetter resin degrades in the barrel, which causes splay and brittle snap features. Dryer inlet: Quillan 0.11–0.14%; Arnholt 0.27–0.33%. D7 outlet (dew point −42 °C): Quillan 0.05%, Arnholt 0.07%. D5 outlet (dew point −16 to −19 °C): Quillan 0.13–0.16%, Arnholt 0.25–0.31%. Wk 42 day-shift trial: Arnholt lot A-2291 was dried in portable dryer PD-1 (−40 °C) and fed to Press 5. It measured 0.08% at the throat and gave 0.8% rejects on 2,400 parts. The same lot run through D5 on the previous day shift gave 10.4% rejects. Caveat: every Arnholt sample came from octabins held in the north annex and every Quillan sample from bags in the main warehouse. No Arnholt material has been held in conditioned storage.

catalogue.title: Supplier audit report on Arnholt Resins compounding site, June
catalogue.text: Audit of the Arnholt Resins compounding site, 11 June. Scope: quality management system, lot traceability, change control, calibration, packaging and labelling. Findings: one minor non-conformance (two gauges in the finished-goods warehouse past their calibration date, corrected during the audit). The lot traceability test passed in 20 minutes. Packaging and labelling conform to Marrowgate requirements. Overall rating: B (approved, routine surveillance). Recommendation: proceed to a production trial subject to part approval. Lead auditor: J. Lindqvist.

catalogue.title: Procurement dual-sourcing business case for PA66-GF30 resin, May
catalogue.text: Quillan list price is up 14% year on year. Arnholt quote is 11% below current Quillan pricing. Target: 50/50 volume split by Q1 next year. catalogue.title: Dryer manufacturer service desk advice on D5 dew-point drift
catalogue.source: Email from dryer manufacturer service desk, week 42
catalogue.text: Re: unit D5, installed 2019. 'On this model, dew points warmer than −30 °C usually mean either a failing regeneration heater or exhausted desiccant, sometimes both. Without a site visit we can't tell you which. For a unit of this age our standard recommendation is to replace the heater element and the desiccant together, then recheck the dew point after 24 hours. We would not advise widening the alarm limit beyond −30 °C.'

hypotheses.text: Resin from the new supplier, Arnholt, is defective and produces the VX rejects whichever press and dryer it is run through.
Degraded drying in D5 produces the VX rejects whichever supplier's resin it is drying.
The VX rejects come from Arnholt resin being dried in D5 while D5 is degraded. Neither the new resin nor the degraded dryer raises rejects on its own.
Errors by the six operators who joined second shift in week 36 produce the VX rejects.

actions.text: Put the six operators who joined second shift in week 36 on formal performance improvement plans and take them off VX production until they are re-certified.

Repair D5 (regeneration heater and desiccant) and confirm its dew point is back to −40 °C. Restore the original D5 alarm limit. Until D5 is verified, keep Arnholt lots off D5 by routing them to Press 7 or drying them in a verified dryer. Add a feed-throat moisture check for every VX resin lot.
As the only response, send all Arnholt lots to Press 7 and run Press 5 on Quillan resin only, leaving D5 and its alarm limit as they are.

Move all Arnholt octabins out of the north annex into the conditioned main warehouse, renting outside space for the finished goods this displaces, to lower the moisture of Arnholt resin reaching the dryers.

truth.groundTruthNarrative: The VX reject rise needs two conditions at once. Dryer D5 has been degraded since late July (failing regeneration heater, overdue desiccant), and its alarm was relaxed in week 31. Quillan resin arrives dry enough (0.11–0.14%) that even the weak D5 brings it below the 0.20% molding limit (0.13–0.16%), so Press 5 ran normally through August. Arnholt resin, released to both presses in week 37, arrives much wetter (0.27–0.33%). That is still within Arnholt's own 0.35% certificate spec. The healthy D7 dries it to 0.07%, which is why the Press 7 trial and later Press 7 production were clean. D5 cannot dry it: Arnholt leaves D5 at 0.25–0.31%, and the wet nylon degrades in the barrel, giving splay and brittle latches. Rejects are about 10% in the Press 5/Arnholt cell and under 1% in every other cell. Drying the same Arnholt lot in a portable dryer and molding it on Press 5 removed the rejects. The second-shift excess is an artefact: Press 7 runs VX only on first shift, so all second-shift VX comes from Press 5. Within each press-and-resin cell, new hires perform the same as experienced operators. Why Arnholt resin is wetter, whether from the supplier or from storage in the humid annex, is not established. The fix is to restore D5 and its alarm and to contain Arnholt away from D5 until it is verified.

answers.rationale: Arnholt resin ran at 0.7% rejects in the Press 7 trial (E3). It ran at 0.8% on Press 7 in production, weeks 37–42 (C1). Dried in PD-1, it gave 0.8% even on Press 5 (C2). The claim that Arnholt produces rejects whichever press and dryer it goes through is therefore contradicted.

D5 was degraded from late July, yet rejects stayed at 0.7–0.8% through weeks 30–36 (E1, E4). Press 5 on Quillan ran at 0.9% in weeks 37–42 (C1), and D5 brings Quillan below the limit (C2). Degraded drying alone does not produce the rejects.

C1 shows rejects confined to the Press 5/Arnholt cell (9.9%), with the other three cells at 0.7–0.9%. C2 supplies the mechanism: only Arnholt dried in D5 exceeds the moisture limit. C2 also gives an intervention: the same Arnholt lot dried properly on Press 5 gave 0.8% rejects. From the initial file alone this is live but unestablished, because there is no breakdown by press and resin.

The second-shift excess in E1 is confounded by press: all second-shift VX is made on Press 5 (C1). Within each press-and-resin cell, first and second shift match (9.7% vs 10.1%; 0.9% vs 0.9%). New hires match experienced operators (9.9% vs 10.3% on Arnholt, 0.9% vs 0.9% on Quillan).

Arnholt leaves D5 at 0.25–0.31% but leaves D7 at 0.07%. Quillan leaves D5 at 0.13–0.16%. The same Arnholt lot dried in PD-1 measured 0.08%. Covariation, mechanism and a direct dryer substitution establish the link. Without C2 there is no moisture data.

The datasheet mechanism, the fact that only the over-limit cell has high rejects, and the PD-1 intervention (same lot and press: 10.4% when wet vs 0.8% when dried) establish causation (C2). C1 rules out the main rival, operators, and shows the reject-code mix is unchanged.

The timing and the shift difference make the link look associated in the initial file. C1 counts against the link itself: new hires running Quillan on Press 5 have 0.9% rejects, and on Arnholt they are no worse than experienced operators.

Resin held in the annex (all of it Arnholt) is wetter at the dryer inlet than resin held in the main warehouse (all of it Quillan). But storage location is perfectly confounded with supplier, and C2 notes that no Arnholt material has been held in conditioned storage. Annex humidity (C7) makes the link plausible but does not separate it from supplier origin.

C1 shows the new hires perform no worse than experienced operators. Disciplining them punishes the wrong party and does nothing about the Press 5/Arnholt rejects under the supported hypothesis. No live rival makes it useful.

This removes the failing condition (D5), restores the protective alarm that was relaxed in week 31, and contains the risky combination until D5 is verified. It also adds a moisture check that would catch wet resin from either supplier. It does not depend on whether the D5 fault is the heater or the desiccant, because it addresses both.

C1 and C2 show Arnholt is fine on Press 7 and Quillan is fine on Press 5, so this stops the rejects. But it leaves D5 degraded with a relaxed alarm and thin margin (Quillan leaves D5 at 0.13–0.16% against a 0.20% limit). It is reasonable but clearly inferior to A2.

This would help if annex storage is what makes Arnholt resin wet, but that is only an association confounded with supplier (R4). If Arnholt resin arrives wet, the move costs rental and disruption without lasting harm. Committing to it now is not justified.

The highest-ranked action is A2. The cross-tab (C1) and the moisture measurements with the dryer-substitution trial (C2) together establish the interaction and show that restoring drying removes the rejects, so committing to A2 is justified. The unresolved storage question does not affect A2.

truth.authoringNotes: Initial file: each single cause has an apparent contrast case. Arnholt was clean in the Press 7 trial (E3); D5 was degraded while rejects stayed normal on Quillan (E4, E1). The dashboard's shift split plus the week-36 hiring (E1, E2, E5) steers readers toward H4. Without reads, H3 is unknown and H4 looks plausible. C1 alone settles H4 and R3 (the shift confound and the operator comparison); no other item breaks results down by press, resin or operator. C2 alone settles R1, R2 and R4 (moisture data, the intervention, and the storage confound); no other item measures resin moisture. Reading only one leaves either the mechanism edges or the operator trap unresolved. Distractors such as C4, C6, C7, C9, C11, C12 and C14 are plausible requests but change no key: C6, C12 and C14 restate what E4 already says, and C7 gives humidity without any resin measurement. Both A2's routing option and A3 are possible because Press 7 has spare first-shift VX capacity. A4 is the single-cause fix keyed premature.
